evaluation.positioning_hook: A married couples therapist falls into an affair with a client’s husband, then discovers the wife orchestrated the seduction to expose her and destroy her life.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible, adult, and built on sex, betrayal, and blackmail — all reliable thriller fuel. Its audience is narrower than a four-quadrant commercial play because the material is explicitly erotic and psychologically specific, but the hook is strong enough to sell.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening party sequence and keeps sharpening: therapist, affair, client, then the reveal that the wife is controlling the whole trap. The script is easy to pitch in two sentences and the engine is clear from page one.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Pau is a strong lead role because she is competent, vain, lonely, horny, and increasingly unmoored — a full contradiction set. Mare is equally vivid as the controlling, sexually charged antagonist, and Oliver gives the triangle a volatile male pressure point.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to erotic-psychological melodrama without apologizing for it, and the opera motif gives it a distinct high-gloss identity. The late reveal that the wife is the architect of the seduction is a confident, commercial twist rather than a generic affair story.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through reversals: party flirtation, secret affair, professional exposure, surveillance, confrontation, and the final domestic trap. The third act in particular keeps tightening the vise with the office ambush, the bathroom showdown, and the car crash.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels familiar in the best way — a marriage thriller — but the specific configuration of therapist, client, husband, and wife-as-puppeteer makes it feel ownable. The ending lands because the emotional logic of control and projection has been seeded throughout the script.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Manhattan high-rise, therapy office, Upper East Side marriage, and Hudson weekend house create a polished social world with class and status baked in. It is not an expansive world, but it is textured enough to generate story and status pressure at every turn.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific register: glossy, erotic, anxious, and operatic. The repeated use of Mozart and the polished domestic surfaces give it a signature tone that separates it from more generic affair thrillers.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the sex-and-blackmail engine, the script is really about control, projection, shame, and the fantasy of being seen. The final divorce and therapy beats suggest a deeper emotional afterlife, though the script mostly keeps that depth in service of the thriller.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Pau/Mare/Oliver triangle is highly generative, and Anders adds a second domestic pressure system that keeps the story from collapsing into a single affair thread. Nearly every pairing in the script produces tension, leverage, or erotic charge.

lead_characters.name: Paulina Cuevas Ström
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 40s, Spanish-born, married, upper-middle-class Manhattan therapist.
lead_characters.hook: A polished couples therapist who lives by control, presentation, and professional authority until desire, shame, and manipulation strip those defenses away. Pau is intelligent and self-aware enough to diagnose everyone else, but not herself; her arc is powered by the gap between the composed woman she performs and the impulsive woman she keeps trying to deny.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Nicole Kidman in Big Little Lies — a controlled, elegant woman whose interior fracture keeps widening until the performance has to carry erotic charge, humiliation, panic, and survival in the same role.

lead_characters.name: Meredith Adler
lead_characters.hook: A razor-edged lawyer who reads as polished, ambitious, and socially fluent, but is actually the most dangerous person in the room. Mare weaponizes intelligence, sexuality, and composure with the calm of someone who believes control is a birthright, not a tactic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Rosamund Pike in Gone Girl — a cool, exacting predator role that lets an actor play intelligence, menace, erotic control, and emotional volatility without ever losing the mask.

lead_characters.name: Oliver Ramos
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 40s, affluent finance/private equity professional, married.
lead_characters.hook: A handsome, polished husband who initially reads as flirtatious and evasive, then reveals himself as needy, manipulative, and deeply compromised. Oliver is the kind of man who can look harmless in a room and become frightening the moment his need for control is threatened.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Matthew McConaughey in True Detective season 1 — a charismatic, sexually charged man whose charm is inseparable from menace, self-deception, and a slow collapse of control.

lead_characters.name: Anders Ström
lead_characters.hook: Pau’s emotionally muted husband, who seems passive and slightly underpowered until the script reveals how observant and retaliatory he really is. Anders is the quiet domestic counterweight to the affair plot, and his late reveal as the reporter adds a cold, personal sting.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Stuhlbarg in a prestige domestic drama — a deceptively soft-spoken husband role that pays off in hurt, intelligence, and a late-breaking moral reversal.

lead_characters.name: Sylvie Porter
lead_characters.hook: Pau’s breezy, sexually frank friend who opens the movie in the social world of the wealthy and emotionally compromised. She’s not the engine, but she helps define the script’s class-and-marriage ecosystem and gives Pau a social mirror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Laura Dern in a sharp prestige ensemble — a scene-stealing friend role with wit, status, and just enough bite to feel lived-in.

lead_characters.name: Bill Porter
lead_characters.hook: A genial, slightly drunk host whose flirtation and obliviousness help establish the script’s world of permissive wealth and marital rot. He’s mostly a social texture character, but he gives the opening party its lived-in hypocrisy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Richard Jenkins in a prestige ensemble — a warm, compromised husband role that can carry comic discomfort and quiet sadness.

lead_characters.name: Jackson
lead_characters.hook: Pau’s younger office colleague, a useful pressure valve for the professional world around her. He’s a clean supporting role that helps ground the office environment and later becomes part of the hearing fallout.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a strong character actor like Jake Lacy — a polished, lightly comic professional role that can turn uneasy when the story darkens.

lead_characters.name: Fidan
lead_characters.hook: One half of the recurring couples-therapy material, Fidan gives Pau a credible professional arena and a glimpse of what competent work looks like before the affair unravels her life. She also helps establish Pau’s authority early.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a strong indie performer in a grounded relationship scene — emotionally specific, but not star-dependent.

lead_characters.name: Kunter
lead_characters.hook: Fidan’s partner, skeptical and wounded, whose scenes with Pau establish the therapist’s professional competence and the script’s interest in projection and mistrust. He’s functional but still vivid enough to feel like a real patient.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a reliable character actor in a therapy-scene role — the kind of part that rewards precision and emotional restraint.

lead_characters.name: Mare's Therapist
lead_characters.hook: A later-stage professional mirror who appears only briefly but helps close the loop on Pau’s own recovery and the script’s therapy framework. She’s a functional framing device rather than a major character.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a small but elegant prestige cameo — a role that lands through authority and calm rather than size.

casting_characteristics: One teenage son appears in family-photo and phone references
Lead requires an actor who can play erotic charge, shame, panic, and controlled intelligence
Mare and Oliver need strong chemistry and a believable affluent-married-couple surface
Supporting roles skew 30s-60s and are castable with character actors

notable_requirements: Therapy office with glass-walled executive office counterpart
Four Seasons-style hotel room and hallway
Hudson weekend house and Hudson town exteriors
Law office floor and executive office

technical.vfx_details: No visual effects requirements beyond simple screen inserts and phone UI moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical crash sequence, airbag deployment, blood makeup, bruising, and a few physical struggle beats in the bathroom and office.

rights_flags.detail: Mozart's Queen of the Night aria is used as a recurring, plot-signature musical motif.
LinkedIn, Instagram, academia.edu, Nespresso, Friday Cafe, Four Seasons, and Tanqueray are named on the page.
Freud is referenced and a Freud bust is a recurring prop, though not a depiction of a living person.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult erotic thriller for streaming-first or specialty theatrical.

budget.note: Contemporary Manhattan and Hudson locations keep it grounded, but the multi-location footprint, night work, hotel interiors, and car crash sequence will keep this above a lean contained indie.

casting.note: The lead needs a performer who can carry erotic tension, humiliation, and psychological unraveling without losing authority, and Mare needs a similarly strong counterweight to make the final confrontation land.

development.note: The script is clear and commercially legible, but the final-act escalation into surveillance, coercion, and the domestic reveal depends on precise tonal control to stay thrilling rather than melodramatic.

comp_set.title: Fatal Attraction
comp_set.why_it_comps: The affair-as-catastrophe engine and marital fallout echo the same adult-thriller DNA, with desire turning into threat.

comp_set.title: Gone Girl
comp_set.why_it_comps: The wife-as-strategist reveal and the weaponization of marriage, image, and performance are directly in this lane.

comp_set.title: The Undoing
comp_set.why_it_comps: Upper-class New York marriage pressure, sexual secrecy, and prestige-thriller polish make this a close tonal and audience neighbor.

comp_set.title: Big Little Lies
comp_set.why_it_comps: Female power games, marital rot, and glossy prestige packaging align with the script’s emotional and commercial lane.

comp_set.title: The Girl on the Train
comp_set.why_it_comps: Psychological instability, unreliable intimacy, and a woman caught in a dangerous domestic web fit the same adult thriller audience.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige relationship thrillers with sex, betrayal, and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, skewing female but with meaningful adult male interest; upscale streamer and specialty-theatrical viewers who respond to glossy psychological suspense.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary settings, limited VFX, and a mostly dialogue-driven cast keep it in indie feature territory, though the Manhattan/Hudson footprint and crash sequence prevent true microbudget treatment.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult, glossy, psychologically charged thriller lane where performance, sex, and social status are the selling points. The script is built for buyers who want a star-driven female lead and a clean, high-concept hook that can be marketed on premise alone.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional and narrative arc; no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the central triangle.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hook is immediate and marketable.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a clean buyer pitch and a trailer-ready premise that can be understood in one breath. That makes it attractive to streamer dev execs and specialty distributors looking for an adult thriller with a sharp logline.
strengths.evidence: The opening party flirtation turns into an affair with a client’s husband, then flips into the reveal that the wife engineered the trap.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Pau is a real lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The role can attract an actor who wants a prestige showcase with erotic tension, shame, and psychological unraveling rather than a generic victim part. That is exactly the kind of part that can elevate a mid-budget thriller into a star vehicle.
strengths.evidence: Pau moves from controlled therapist to compulsive affair partner to panicked professional under investigation, with each phase visible on the page.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Mare is the movie’s secret weapon.
strengths.what_it_means: A female antagonist with intelligence, sexual control, and strategic patience gives the script a memorable engine and a strong casting conversation. Buyers respond to a villain who is not just dangerous but fascinating.
strengths.evidence: Mare reveals she orchestrated the seduction, controls Oliver, and turns the therapy room into a trap.

strengths.what_it_means: The script knows exactly what lane it wants and stays in it, which helps commercial positioning and audience expectation. That clarity is valuable for buyers who want a confident adult genre play rather than a timid prestige drama.
strengths.evidence: The hotel-room encounters, office sex, bathroom confrontation, and final threesome reveal all escalate the same charged register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opera motif gives it identity.
strengths.what_it_means: The recurring Mozart cue and the polished, high-gloss surfaces create a signature that can be marketed visually and sonically. That kind of motif helps a thriller feel authored rather than generic.
strengths.evidence: Opera plays over black, returns in Pau’s earbuds, and crescendos through the final montage and ending.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The triangle keeps generating new pressure.
strengths.what_it_means: The Pau/Mare/Oliver dynamic creates a durable engine for escalation, reversals, and shifting alliances. That gives the script strong momentum and makes the third act feel like a payoff rather than a detour.
strengths.evidence: Every major scene reconfigures who has leverage: the office reveal, the hotel confrontations, the bathroom trap, and the final violence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The class world is legible and useful.
strengths.what_it_means: Upper East Side money, Hudson weekends, therapy culture, and polished professional status give the story a premium sheen that buyers know how to market. It also widens the appeal beyond pure sex-thriller audiences into prestige-drama viewers.
strengths.evidence: The penthouse party, therapy office, law office, brownstone, and Hudson house all reinforce a specific affluent social ecosystem.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, adult thriller package: a star-making lead role, a memorable female antagonist, and a premise that can be sold in one sentence. The contemporary, mostly dialogue-driven production footprint keeps it in indie feature territory, which makes the script especially attractive to streamer buyers and prestige genre financiers looking for a glossy, performance-forward play.

items.area: The final-act escalation is tonally extreme.
items.detail: The move from affair thriller into coercion, surveillance, bathroom violence, and a near-strangulation in Pau’s office is bold, but it pushes the material into a very specific hard-edged lane. That is a real commercial strength for some buyers and a real sensitivity for others, especially if they want prestige polish without the most explicit sexual and physical violence.

items.area: The movie depends on a very specific lead performance.
items.detail: Pau has to play controlled, erotic, ashamed, funny, and unraveling without losing audience sympathy, and that is a narrow casting lane. The script is strongest when that role is magnetic; without the right actor, the whole piece reads more brittle than intended.

items.area: The story is built around a narrow adult audience.
items.detail: This is not a broad four-quadrant play; the explicit sex, marital betrayal, and psychological manipulation point squarely at adult thriller buyers. That is fine, but it means the commercial ceiling is tied to prestige streaming and specialty theatrical rather than mass-market reach.

items.area: The named-music motif adds clearance work.
items.detail: Mozart’s Queen of the Night aria is a recurring signature element, so the music is not just flavor — it is part of the script’s identity. That means sync and usage planning will matter early if the production wants to preserve the opera-driven branding.

issues.headline: The main buyer conversation will be about how far they want to go with the erotic-psychological escalation, because the script commits hard to coercion, humiliation, and violence in the back half. The other real friction points are casting Pau correctly and deciding whether the adult-only lane and named-opera motif fit the intended release strategy.
